newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. State welfare battle seen hurting localities.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. State welfare battle seen hurting localities.

text.p: New York State Gov George Pataki and the Assembly have put out very different welfare plans and likely face a long battle, though delays could hurt localities, city and advocacy officials said on Wednesday.

"The state's failure to act puts the city in a position of navigating without a compass," said Thomas McMahon, the New York City Council's finance director. "Successful welfare reform requires planning and you need to need to develop the strategies."

Noting that in less than four months the city has to start putting new welfare rules in place, the Council's Committee on General Welfare plans to hold hearings on Thursday to examine how the city is handling its workfare program and other issues. The new federal welfare program starts on July 1, and the state must adapt its program by that deadline.

New York City, which has the state's vast majority of welfare recipients and immigrants, is particularly vulnerable under the new rules, as they impose stiff new work requirements and halt some benefits for legal immigrants. Illegal immigrants have never been paid benefits.

The state last year set a national record for late budgets and neither legislative leaders nor Pataki have expressed much optimism that it will do substantially better this year. The budget was due on April 1, and Albany has approved a contingency budget to carry it through May 9.

Rus Sykes, executive director of the State Community Aid Association in Albany, estimated it would take localities three to four months to implement new changes agreed to by the Republican governor and the Assembly, which is controlled by Democrats.
"We're already behind the curve with some significant implementation problems...If they wait until June 30 to do it, it's going to have negative effects for everyone in the system," said Sykes.

The Assembly's new welfare plan was quickly blasted by the Republican governor, who said that it would "undo" workfare programs that oblige those who get benefits to work, and fail to meet the federal program that was signed into law last August. A spokeswoman for Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, was not immediately available to comment.

But the Assembly's program satisfied a number of the concerns raised by advocates for the poor, who liked its plan to continue for two years cash benefits for single, able-bodied adults, which Pataki would halt and instead assist such individuals with a voucher system.

"In general, their approach represents, I think, a much more reasonable approach. If anything, they may have invested a little too much in child care," Sykes said. He also wanted bigger exemptions from some time limits.
